introduction: The guide remembers the first Muslim generation as ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and Bahá’u’lláh told it to different hearers: two tribes at war for centuries made brothers; thirteen years of persecution in Mecca and the migration; the trench, the spoils of Hunayn and the fate of the Banu Qurayzah, which ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says distressed him from childhood; the dispute at the Prophet’s deathbed and the words “Sufficient unto us is the Book of God”; Karbala; and smaller stories of caliphs, a holy fool and a tethered camel. The Qur’an’s own verses stand beside the events they refer to: enemies made brothers, “Grieve not, God is with us”, the sanction to fight and its limit, the worth of a single soul. From the Bible come the parallels any founding has: a strife about who is greatest, parties named for apostles, disciples who walk away, a friend who swears he will die and flees. And there are voices that press on the hard places: “put up thy sword”, “vengeance is mine”, Montaigne on who is called barbarous. Carlyle and Gibbon, outsiders both, are here for what they conceded.
questions: The Qur’an says of the tribes of Medina, “ye were enemies and He made friendship between your hearts”, and Paul says a wall was broken down. What do the readings credit with that change, and what do they show of how fragile it was?

“Sanction is given unto those who fight because they have been wronged … but begin not hostilities”; “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.” How does reading 12 account for the difference, and what does it leave unsettled?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá records his own lasting distress at the account of the Banu Qurayzah. What does his example suggest about how to remember violence in a history one reveres?

The disciples strove over who was greatest, and Corinth split into parties. Does every religious community meet the question of succession, and what do the readings think was lost when it was answered with “the Book is sufficient”?
Husayn is called victorious in defeat, and the caliphs forgotten in their success. By what measure do the readings, Shelley and the Preacher judge what lasts?

outside.why: Aws and Khazraj, at war for generations, become brothers. This is the Qur’an’s own verse on it: ye were enemies and He made friendship between your hearts, so that ye became as brothers by His grace.
Paul says the like of Jew and Gentile in the first churches: he hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition.
An Orb of Guidance had risen from the horizon of Mecca. Isaiah to another city: arise, shine; for thy light is come.
The Arabs before and after. Carlyle, the first prominent English writer to defend Muhammad’s sincerity, saw in him a silent great soul, one of those who cannot but be in earnest.

“Barbaric, more ignorant than animals.” Montaigne warns that each calls barbarous whatever is not his own custom; the Arabs of that age had their poetry, their hospitality and their law of protection. How much of the darkness is needed to tell the story of the dawn?
A boy of eleven meets a Christian monk. Luke’s boy of twelve sits among the teachers, hearing them and asking questions.
Thirteen years of torment in Mecca. Paul on the first apostles: troubled on every side, yet not distressed; persecuted, but not forsaken.
Someone offered bloodshed as proof of greatness. Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
The migration to Medina, from which the calendar is counted. Abraham went out, not knowing whither he went.
The reading quotes this verse of the cave: when he said unto his comrade, Grieve not. Lo! God is with us.
A trench dug under siege. Nehemiah’s builders worked with one hand and with the other held a weapon.
In one day a whole clan apostatized. From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. Will ye also go away?
He sanctioned war “for the preservation of the lives of His followers”. The verse: sanction is given unto those who fight because they have been wronged.
And its limit: fight in the way of God against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities.

Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword. Jesus never held a city; Muhammad did. Does that difference answer the contrast, or only explain it?
Augustine, writing to a Christian general: peace should be the object of your desire; war should be waged only as a necessity, that peace may be obtained.
After Hunayn the spoils go to the newly reconciled, and the old companions murmur. The labourers hired first murmur too: is thine eye evil, because I am good?
A pact broken in wartime, and a terrible judgment. The law of Moses for cities given as an inheritance was harsher still. What was the standard of the age, and by what standard do we now judge both?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that as a child he read of the Banu Qurayzah and was distressed beyond words. The Qur’an gives the measure of such distress: whoso slew a soul, it shall be as if he had slain mankind altogether.
Nine hundred beheaded in two days. Paul: avenge not yourselves; vengeance is mine, saith the Lord. The readings report the event without softening it; what does the guide ask us to do with it?
At Ghadír-i-Khumm the Prophet raises ‘Alí before the people. Moses is told to take Joshua, set him before the congregation, and put some of his honour upon him.
“Division first appeared in the house of the Prophet”, at his deathbed. At the last supper there was a strife among the disciples, which of them should be accounted the greatest.
“The first breach in Islam.” Within a generation of Jesus: I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas. Is Christ divided?

“Sufficient unto us is the Book of God.” Christians know the dispute as scripture alone against scripture with an authorized interpreter. Paul: the letter killeth. Can any book be sufficient without someone to say what it means?
Even the killers at Karbala “made mention of Him with words”. Isaiah: this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me.
A cleric who always sighed “would that I had been with you” takes to his heels at the test. Peter: though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee. Likewise also said all the disciples.
Husayn at Karbala, his body torn, “was still victorious”. Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
Gibbon, no friend of enthusiasm, wrote that in a distant age and climate the tragic scene of the death of Hosein will awaken the sympathy of the coldest reader.
The site was ploughed for eighty years, and people still said: it was here. The stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it.
Thirty-six caliphs, and no trace of any. “My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings”: round the decay of that colossal wreck the lone and level sands stretch far away.

Bahlul the holy fool is remembered when caliphs are not. The Preacher tells of a poor wise man who delivered a city, yet no man remembered that same poor man. Which is the rule and which the exception?
Asked how to keep his camel safe, the Prophet is remembered as answering: tie her, and trust in God. Proverbs: the horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the Lord.
The Prophet’s own uncle is among the besiegers. A man’s foes shall be they of his own household.
Hajjaj prays at the mirror that his character be as fair as his face, and his wife laughs. James’s man beholds his natural face in a glass and straightway forgets what manner of man he was.
Abu Jahl’s hands at the Prophet’s throat in the Kaaba. Stephen was dragged from the council and stoned.

shortfall: Two anecdotes (the doubters at the trench, and the tale of Nu‘man and Mu‘ayth) are told for their own sake and were left without companions.
